B6b-02-bone-structure-osteon

Two diagrams side by side. Left: a long bone (femur) cut lengthwise, showing the shaft (diaphysis) of thick compact bone around a marrow cavity with yellow marrow, the two enlarged ends (epiphyses) of spongy bone with red marrow, the growth plates, the articular cartilage covering each end, the periosteum on the outside, and a blood vessel entering the bone. Right: an enlarged transverse section of compact bone showing several Haversian systems, each with a central Haversian canal containing a blood vessel, concentric lamellae, osteocytes in lacunae and fine canaliculi radiating out.
B6b-10-synovial-joint-cross-section

Longitudinal section through a typical synovial joint (e.g. the knee, simplified), showing the ends of two bones covered with smooth blue articular cartilage, the joint cavity filled with pale yellow synovial fluid, the synovial membrane lining the inside of the capsule, the fibrous joint capsule, ligaments on the outside joining bone to bone, and a muscle with its tendon attached to one bone.
B6b-07-mammalian-vertebrae-comparison

A row of four vertebrae drawn from the front and from the side, for comparison: (1) a thoracic vertebra with a long backward-pointing neural spine, a medium centrum with capitular facets, and short transverse processes with tubercular facets, with the head and tubercle of a rib shown fitting into these facets; (2) a lumbar vertebra with a very large centrum, broad flat neural spine and long broad transverse processes; (3) the sacrum, a triangular bone of fused vertebrae with wing-like transverse processes joining the ilium; (4) a caudal vertebra reduced to a small rod-like centrum.
B6b-12-antagonistic-arm-muscles

Two side-by-side diagrams of the human arm showing antagonistic muscles. Left ("arm bent"): the biceps on the front of the upper arm drawn short and bulging (contracted, in red), the triceps behind drawn long and thin (relaxed, in light pink), the forearm raised; tendons connecting the biceps to the scapula and radius and the triceps to the scapula/humerus and the olecranon process of the ulna. Right ("arm straight"): triceps short and fat (contracted), biceps long and thin (relaxed), forearm lowered. Mark the elbow joint as a fulcrum with a small triangle.
B6b-13-skeletal-disorders-comparison

A row of four simple diagrams of skeletal problems: (1) a child's legs bowed outwards from rickets beside a normal pair of legs; (2) a long bone with a simple (closed) fracture under intact skin beside a compound (open) fracture with bone ends breaking through the skin; (3) a knee joint with worn, rough articular cartilage and narrowed joint space (arthritis) beside a healthy knee joint; (4) a forearm held straight on a splint with a bandage as first aid.
B6b-01-insect-exoskeleton-anatomy

Two side-by-side diagrams. Left: a vertical section through an insect exoskeleton showing (from outside to inside) the thin waxy epicuticle, the hard dark exocuticle, the softer endocuticle, a layer of epidermal cells and the basement membrane, with a muscle attached to an apodeme on the inside, and a thin flexible joint membrane between two hard sclerites. Right: a grasshopper or cockroach in outline, with its jointed exoskeleton drawn as hard plates, beside an old split cuticle left after moulting.
B6b-03-human-skeleton-front-view

Front view of the complete human skeleton standing upright, with the axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) coloured pale blue and the appendicular skeleton (girdles and limbs) coloured pale yellow.
B6b-04-human-skull-lateral-view

Side view of a human skull showing the cranium with the zigzag sutures between its bones, the orbit, the nasal cavity, the maxilla with upper teeth, the mandible with lower teeth hinged to the cranium near the ear opening, the zygomatic arch, and at the base the foramen magnum and occipital condyle (drawn slightly from below to show them).
B6b-11-types-synovial-joints

Four small labelled diagrams of synovial joint types arranged in a 2×2 grid, each with a simple mechanical analogy icon beside it. (1) Ball and socket: the head of the femur in the acetabulum of the hip, with arrows in all directions, and a toy ball-in-cup icon. (2) Hinge: the elbow with the humerus and ulna, with a curved arrow in one plane, and a door-hinge icon. (3) Pivot: the atlas rotating around the odontoid process of the axis, with a circular arrow, and a door-key-in-lock icon. (4) Gliding: wrist carpal bones sliding over each other, with small sliding arrows, and two flat plates icon.
B6b-05-human-vertebral-column

Side view of the human vertebral column showing its S-shaped curves, with the five regions coloured differently and bracketed: cervical (7), thoracic (12, with stubs of ribs attached), lumbar (5, largest vertebrae), sacral (5 fused, sacrum) and caudal (4 fused, coccyx). Show the intervertebral discs as pale blue pads between vertebrae and the skull outline at the top.
B6b-06-cervical-vertebrae-comparison

Front-and-top views of three cervical vertebrae side by side: (1) the atlas, ring-shaped with no centrum, wide wing-like transverse processes, large articular facets for the occipital condyles and a large neural canal; (2) the axis, with the peg-like odontoid process sticking up from its centrum and a large blade-like neural spine; (3) a typical cervical vertebra with a small centrum, short neural spine, wide neural canal and transverse processes each pierced by a vertebrarterial canal.
B6b-09-pectoral-pelvic-girdles

Two diagrams side by side. Left: the human pectoral girdle and right forelimb seen from the front: scapula with glenoid cavity and acromion, clavicle joining the sternum, humerus, radius and ulna (with olecranon process at the elbow), carpals, metacarpals and phalanges. Right: the human pelvic girdle and right hindlimb from the front: the pelvis with ilium, ischium, pubis, acetabulum, obturator foramen, pubic symphysis and the sacrum between the two ilia; femur with head and trochanter, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals (with calcaneus), metatarsals and phalanges.
B6b-08-human-rib-cage

Front view of the human rib cage showing the thoracic vertebrae at the back, 12 pairs of ribs curving round to the front, the sternum with manubrium, body and xiphoid process, the costal cartilages in pale blue joining the ribs to the sternum, and the two floating ribs at the bottom. Brackets mark true ribs (1 to 7), false ribs (8 to 10) and floating ribs (11 to 12). Add a small side inset showing the rib cage moving up and out during inspiration (arrows) with the diaphragm flattening.
